\chapter{Lo --- Saying It Without Naming It}
\label{ch:pronoun-lo}
\hlchaptermodality{70}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can replace a masculine noun already named with lo, in front of the verb.}

Complete ES-C42-lo: turn Tengo el libro into Lo tengo, and name the article that shares lo's Latin ancestor.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[lo]{lo — \textquotedblleft{}it\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:ES-C42-lo}



\begin{quote}
Say \textquotedblleft{}my name is\textquotedblright{} in Spanish. (\emph{Me llamo}.) Where does that little \emph{me} sit — before the verb, or after it?
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: a slot you have been using all along}]
Before the verb. You have known that since your fourth chapter, and you have been doing it every time you say your name.

Here is a second word for that same slot.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{lo} — \emph{it}, standing in for something masculine.
\end{quote}

Watch what it does:

\begin{quote}
\emph{Tengo \textbf{el libro}.} — I have the book. \emph{\textbf{Lo} tengo.} — I have it.
\end{quote}

The noun leaves; \emph{lo} takes its place; and it goes where \emph{me} goes — in front of the verb. Not one new rule. One new word for a slot you already own.

Notice that this only became possible last chapter. A pronoun replaces a noun, so it needs a noun to replace — which is why these three ordinary words came first.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{Lo} should look faintly familiar, and it should also look wrong. It is almost \emph{el}, but not quite. That is not a coincidence, and the near-miss has a cause.

Latin \emph{ille}, \textquotedblleft{}that one,\textquotedblright{} changed shape depending on the job it was doing. As the \textbf{object} of a verb it was \textbf{illum}. Spanish got both its article and its object pronoun out of that one word — and then wore it down twice, differently, because the two jobs put the stress in different places:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Leaning on a noun, unstressed, it lost its vowel: \emph{illum $\to$ elo $\to$ \textbf{el}}.
  \item Standing alone in the verb's slot, it kept the vowel: \emph{illum $\to$ \textbf{lo}}.
\end{itemize}

So \emph{el} and \emph{lo} are the same ancient word, split by the work it was asked to do. English did something similar with \emph{he} and \emph{him}: one word, two shapes, and the shape tells you the job.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Tengo el libro\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}Lo tengo\textquotedblright{} — hear the noun disappear
  \item \textquotedblleft{}me llamo\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}lo tengo\textquotedblright{} — the same slot, twice
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{lo} mean? (\textbf{It} — for something masculine.) Where does it go? (\textbf{Before} the verb.) Next: the same job, done by a word that never changed its shape at all.
\end{tcolorbox}
